abstraction.definition: Leaving out features of a reasoning scenario that do not matter for the question we are studying.

algorithm.definition: A precise, step-by-step procedure that takes an input and produces an output in finitely many steps.

axiom.definition: A formula accepted as a starting point in a proof system or theory.

belief-revision.definition: Changing the propositions we accept when we receive new information, including information that conflicts with earlier beliefs.

bivalence.definition: The assumption that each formula has exactly one of the two Boolean truth-values, true or false.

boolean-function.definition: A function that takes a fixed number of Boolean values, 0 and 1, as inputs and returns one Boolean value.

bound-variable.definition: An occurrence of a variable governed by the nearest enclosing quantifier for that variable.

cardinality.definition: The number of elements of a set.

clause.definition: A disjunctive clause is a disjunction of literals. A conjunctive clause is a conjunction of literals. A single literal counts as either. In resolution, an unqualified clause means a disjunctive clause.

classical-logic.definition: The logical framework used in our Boolean and FOL chapters, with bivalent semantics and classical inference principles.

completeness.definition: A proof system is complete if every semantic consequence can be derived in it.

conditional.definition: An if-then statement. In classical logic, A→B is false exactly when A is true and B is false.

conditional-probability.definition: The probability of one claim given another. Formally, Pr(A given B)=Pr(A∧B)/Pr(B), provided Pr(B)>0.

conjunctive-normal-form.definition: A conjunction of disjunctions of literals, abbreviated CNF.

consequence.definition: A conclusion is a logical consequence of premises if every model making the premises true also makes the conclusion true.

constant.definition: A name in a formal language; in an FOL model it denotes an object in the domain.

contradiction.definition: A formula that is false in every model of the logic under discussion.

countermodel.definition: A model in which all the premises of an inference are true and its conclusion is not true.

decision-procedure.definition: An algorithm that terminates on every allowed input with the correct yes-or-no answer.

deductive-closure.definition: The set of all logical consequences of a set of formulas.

deductive-validity.definition: The impossibility of the premises being true and the conclusion false in the reasoning situations under consideration.

denotation.definition: The value of an expression under an interpretation; a term denotes an object, with variable values supplied by an assignment.

derivability.definition: The existence of a formal proof of a conclusion from given assumptions, written with ⊢.

designated-value.definition: A truth value counted as acceptable in defining a consequence relation; in K3, only 1 is designated.

discharge.definition: Ending a temporary assumption's role as an open assumption by applying a rule that permits it, such as conditional introduction.

disjunction.definition: An or-formula. Classical A∨B is true exactly when at least one disjunct is true, including when both are.

disjunctive-normal-form.definition: A disjunction of conjunctions of literals, abbreviated DNF.

domain.definition: The nonempty set of objects over which an FOL model interprets names, predicates, functions, and quantifiers.

eigenvariable.definition: A fresh name or variable used for an arbitrary object in a quantifier proof, subject to the rule's freshness conditions.

empty-clause.definition: A disjunction with no literals, written ⊥. Its value is 0 under every Boolean valuation.

entailment.definition: Another name for semantic consequence, written with ⊨.

equisatisfiable.definition: Two formulas are equisatisfiable iff they are either both satisfiable or both unsatisfiable.

equivalence.definition: Two formulas are logically equivalent if they have the same truth-value in every model of the logic.

existential-quantifier.definition: The symbol ∃, used to say that at least one object in the domain satisfies a condition.

expansion.definition: Adding a formula and all its consequences together with the old beliefs: KB+A=Cn(KB∪{A}).

explosion.definition: The inference principle that any conclusion follows from a contradiction.

extension.definition: The objects, or tuples of objects, to which a predicate applies in a model.

fair-search.definition: A search strategy that does not postpone any eligible inference forever.

first-order-logic.definition: A logic with names, predicates, function symbols, and quantifiers over objects.

formal-language.definition: A set of finite strings of symbols from an alphabet.

formalization.definition: Representing an expression or inference in a formal language.

formula.definition: An expression formed according to the syntax of a logical language.

free-variable.definition: An occurrence of a variable not governed by a quantifier for that variable.

fuzzy-predicate.definition: A predicate whose extension assigns degrees in [0,1] rather than just membership or nonmembership.

grammar.definition: Rules for generating the expressions of a formal language.

horn-clause.definition: A disjunctive clause containing at most one positive literal.

idealization.definition: Representing a situation in a simplified form that need not reproduce all its real features.

inductive-support.definition: Support that premises give a conclusion without guaranteeing it. In probability models, evidence positively supports a conclusion when learning the evidence raises its probability.

inference.definition: A piece of reasoning from premises to a conclusion.

interpretation.definition: An assignment of meanings to the nonlogical vocabulary of a formal language over a domain.

knowledge-base.definition: A set of statements represented in a formal language, which an agent can ASK for consequences and TELL new information.

knowledge-engineering.definition: Choosing a representation and encoding the information needed for a reasoning task.

literal.definition: An atomic formula or the negation of an atomic formula.

logical-validity.definition: Validity that depends on logical form, rather than the particular subject matter of the inference.

material-validity.definition: Correctness that depends on domain-specific meanings, facts, or assumptions; in inductive reasoning, support relative to a particular probability measure.

model.definition: A mathematical representation of a possible reasoning situation; a model of premises makes those premises true.

model-checking.definition: Determining whether a formula is true in a specified model.

modus-ponens.definition: The inference from A → B and A to B.

most-general-unifier.definition: A unifier from which every other unifier is obtained by further substitution.

natural-deduction.definition: A proof system with introduction and elimination rules, including rules for reasoning with and discharging temporary assumptions.

negation.definition: A not-formula. Classical ¬A is true exactly when A is false.

occurs-check.definition: The unification check that rejects replacing a variable by a term containing that same variable properly.

predicate.definition: A symbol expressing a property of objects or a relation among them.

premise.definition: A statement from which an inference starts.

proof.definition: A chaining of inference rules applied to logical formulas, with assumptions tracked through the derivation.

proof-checking.definition: Checking that a supplied formal proof obeys the rules and establishes its stated conclusion from its stated assumptions.

proof-search.definition: Searching for a formal derivation of a conclusion from assumptions.

pseudocode.definition: A precise description of an algorithm written for readers, using programming-like notation without requiring a complete executable program.

refutation.definition: A derivation of a contradiction from a set of formulas, establishing that the set is unsatisfiable.

resolution.definition: An inference rule that removes one complementary pair of literals from two clauses and forms the disjunction of the remaining literals.

satisfiability.definition: A propositional formula is satisfiable iff some Boolean valuation makes it true. A set of formulas is jointly satisfiable iff one Boolean valuation makes all its formulas true.

semantics.definition: The component of a logical system that specifies interpretations and truth conditions.

semidecidability.definition: The availability of a procedure that eventually confirms every positive instance, but may not terminate on a negative instance.

sentence.definition: A formula with no free variables.

skolemization.definition: Replacing existentially quantified variables with fresh witness functions or constants, preserving satisfiability in an expanded language.

soundness.definition: A proof system is sound if everything derivable from assumptions is a semantic consequence of those assumptions.

substitution.definition: Replacing free occurrences of a variable by a term, while avoiding variable capture.

syntax.definition: The component of a logical system that specifies which expressions are well formed.

tactic.definition: An instruction for constructing a proof in a proof assistant, often by reducing a goal to simpler goals.

tautology.definition: A formula true in every valuation of the propositional logic under discussion.

term.definition: An expression for an object, built in FOL from variables, constants, and function symbols.

total-function.definition: A function that assigns exactly one output to every input in its domain.

truth-value.definition: A value assigned to a formula by a semantics, such as 0 or 1 in classical logic.

unification.definition: Finding a substitution that makes two expressions syntactically identical.

universal-quantifier.definition: The symbol ∀, used to say that every object in the domain satisfies a condition.

valuation.definition: A function assigning precisely one Boolean value to every propositional variable of a language.

verification.definition: Checking that a proposed result meets a stated specification; for an argument, checking a proof or a countermodel in the chosen formal setting.

xai.definition: Research into making the behavior and results of AI systems understandable.

conjunction.definition: An and-formula. Classical A∧B is true exactly when both conjuncts are true.

probability.definition: A measure of the chance of an event, given by adding the masses of its outcomes in our finite models.

sample-space.definition: The set of possible outcomes of an experiment, written Ω.

identity.definition: Sameness of objects: a=b is true when the two terms denote the same object.

set.definition: A collection of objects, called its members or elements. Sets are equal when they have exactly the same members.

inductive-validity.definition: In our weak logical sense, conditioning on the premises never lowers the probability of the conclusion, for any distribution giving the premises positive probability.

proof-calculus.definition: A system of rules for constructing logical proofs.

theorem.definition: A mathematical fact whose truth is established by a gapless, rigorous mathematical proof or argument.

curry-howard.definition: The correspondence between propositions and types, and between proofs and terms of those types.

forward-chaining.definition: Starting with known facts and repeatedly applying rules to derive new facts.

backward-chaining.definition: Starting with a goal and searching for rules whose premises would establish it.

factoring.definition: Unifying same-sign literals within a clause and retaining one copy, with the substitution applied to the whole clause.

logic.definition: The discipline that aims to define and understand valid inference.

conclusion.definition: The statement being inferred from the premises of an inference.

validity.definition: In the broad sense used in chapter 1, the premises supporting the conclusion in the way required by the kind of inference under discussion.

inference-indicator.definition: A word or phrase, such as “therefore” or “since”, that signals an inference and helps identify its premises or conclusion.

premise-indicator.definition: A word or phrase, such as “given that”, that signals a premise of an inference.

inference-line.definition: A horizontal line separating the premises above it from the conclusion below it.

inductive-strength.definition: How strongly the premises support a conclusion without guaranteeing it, given the relevant background information.

inductive-validity-in-context.definition: In the sense used in chapter 1, the premises supporting the conclusion strongly enough to justify accepting it, without making it certain.

logical-system.definition: A mathematical model of valid inference, typically comprising syntax, semantics, and proof theory.

proof-theory.definition: The study of formal proofs and the rules by which they are constructed; as a component of a logical system, it models stepwise inference.

logical-law.definition: A general principle of valid inference in a logical system.

counterexample.definition: A case that shows a claim is false. For an inference, it is a case where the premises are true but the conclusion is false.

logical-form.definition: The structure of an expression or inference that matters for logical validity, abstracting from its particular subject matter.

logical-invalidity.definition: An inference being invalid on account of its logical form: some interpretation makes the premises true and the conclusion false.

material-invalidity.definition: An inference admitting a case where the premises are true and the conclusion false, even when the relevant meanings and background facts are respected.

proof-assistant.definition: Software for constructing formal proofs and checking that their steps obey the rules of the proof system.

inference-engine.definition: The part of a reasoning system that applies rules to information in a knowledge base to derive further conclusions.

undecidable-statement.definition: A statement that can neither be proved nor refuted in the theory under discussion.

algorithmic-undecidability.definition: The absence of an algorithm that terminates with the correct yes-or-no answer on every allowed input to a problem.

consistency.definition: A theory is consistent if it does not prove both a statement and its negation.

effective-axiomatization.definition: Specifying the axioms of a theory so that an algorithm can list them all, though the list may be infinite.

conclusion-indicator.definition: A word or phrase, such as “therefore”, that signals the conclusion of an inference.

knowledge-representation-and-reasoning.definition: The study of how to represent information in a form that allows a system to draw conclusions and answer questions.

querying.definition: Asking a database for information by specifying what to retrieve and which conditions it must meet.

system-1.definition: Fast, automatic, intuitive and associative thinking, usually requiring little conscious effort.

system-2.definition: Slow, deliberate and conscious thinking, such as working through a calculation or checking an argument.

set-membership.definition: An object belongs to a set if it is one of its elements, written ∈.

extensional-definition.definition: Specifying a set by listing its elements.

set-abstraction.definition: Specifying a set by a condition its members satisfy, within an intended domain.

alphabet.definition: A set of symbols from which strings of a formal language are formed.

string.definition: A finite sequence of symbols, where order and repetitions matter.

empty-string.definition: The string containing no symbols, often written ε.

kleene-star.definition: For an alphabet Σ, the set Σ* of all finite strings over Σ, including the empty string.

inductive-definition.definition: A definition by initial cases and rules for generating further cases, with nothing else included.

bnf.definition: Notation for grammar rules, using alternatives to specify how expressions can be built.

rewrite-rule.definition: A rule specifying how to replace an expression or a matching part of an expression.

parsing.definition: Reconstructing the grammatical structure of a string according to a grammar.

abstract-syntax-tree.definition: A tree representing the structure of an expression while omitting grammatical details such as brackets.

unique-readability.definition: A property of a grammar: every expression it generates has exactly one grammatical structure.

recursion.definition: Defining or carrying out a procedure through further calls to itself, directly or through other procedures.

operator-precedence.definition: A convention specifying which operators bind more tightly when brackets are omitted.

termination.definition: The property that a procedure finishes after finitely many steps on its intended inputs.

algorithm-correctness.definition: An algorithm produces the specified result on its intended inputs; total correctness also requires termination.

propositional-variable.definition: A basic symbol representing a proposition in a propositional language.

logical-operator.definition: A symbol used to form compound expressions, such as negation or conjunction.

biconditional.definition: A connective written ↔ and read “if and only if”; in classical logic it is true when its two parts have the same truth-value.

auxiliary-symbol.definition: A symbol used to mark the grammatical structure of an expression, such as a bracket in propositional logic.

metavariable.definition: A variable in the language used to talk about another language; for example, A standing for any formula of propositional logic.

rooted-tree.definition: A structure of nodes joined by edges, with a designated root and exactly one path from the root to each other node.

numeral.definition: A written expression representing a number; for example, 120 represents the number one hundred and twenty.

ambiguous-grammar.definition: A grammar that generates at least one expression with more than one grammatical structure.

ambiguity.definition: An expression is ambiguous if it has more than one possible reading.

logical-space.definition: The collection of models considered by a semantics.

proposition.definition: In this semantic approach, the set of models in which a formula is true.

subset.definition: S is a subset of T when every member of S belongs to T. Equality is allowed.

intersection.definition: The set of elements belonging to every one of the sets being intersected.

indefeasible.definition: A consequence that cannot be defeated by adding premises while the semantics remains fixed.

defeasible.definition: An inference whose support can be overturned by additional evidence.

probability-function.definition: A measure assigning events probabilities between 0 and 1. In a finite space, outcome masses sum to 1 and event probabilities sum the masses of their outcomes.

fallacy.definition: An invalid pattern of reasoning that may appear correct.

enumerative-induction.definition: Generalizing from observed instances to a universal claim about a population. The universal claim entails its instances, giving weak logical support; the degree of support and the probability of the conclusion depend on the probability function.

event.definition: A set of outcomes in a probability space. In our logical treatment, propositions are events.

log-likelihood-ratio.definition: The logarithm of the ratio of the likelihood of the evidence under a hypothesis to its likelihood under the alternative. Positive values favor the first hypothesis.

sound-argument.definition: A deductively valid argument with true premises, and therefore a true conclusion. Distinct from soundness of a proof system.

inference-schema.definition: A pattern of premises and conclusion with placeholders for expressions of specified grammatical categories.

modus-tollens.definition: The inference from A → B and ¬B to ¬A, valid classically.

disjunctive-syllogism.definition: The inference from A ∨ B and ¬A to B, valid classically.

affirming-the-consequent.definition: The classically invalid pattern from A → B and B to A.

denying-the-antecedent.definition: The classically invalid pattern from A → B and ¬A to ¬B.

affirming-a-disjunct.definition: The invalid pattern from inclusive A ∨ B and A to ¬B; both disjuncts may be true.

likelihood-ratio.definition: The probability of the evidence if a conclusion is true, divided by its probability if the conclusion is false. Ratios above 1 favor the conclusion; ratios below 1 count against it.

material-support.definition: Inductive support relative to a particular probability function and a chosen measure of support.

logical-support.definition: Support that holds across all probability functions on a fixed model space for which conditioning on the premises is defined, using a specified criterion of support.

meaning-postulate.definition: A statement included among the background assumptions to capture a relationship between the meanings of expressions.

probability-raising.definition: Support measured by the conditional probability of the conclusion given the premises minus its unconditional probability. A positive difference favors the conclusion; a negative difference counts against it.

functional-completeness.definition: A collection of truth-functions is truth-functionally complete if every Boolean truth-function of positive finite arity can be expressed using those functions.

boolean-identity.definition: An equation between Boolean expressions that holds for every assignment of Boolean values to its variables.

de-morgan-laws.definition: The identities NOT (X OR Y) = (NOT X) AND (NOT Y) and NOT (X AND Y) = (NOT X) OR (NOT Y).

binary-representation.definition: Positional notation with digits 0 and 1, in which position n, counted from the right starting at 0, has place value 2 to the power n.

adder.definition: A circuit that computes addition on numbers in binary representation.

half-adder.definition: A circuit that adds two bits, returning a sum bit and a carry bit. The sum is XOR of the inputs and the carry is AND of the inputs.

full-adder.definition: A circuit that adds two bits and an incoming carry, returning a sum bit and an outgoing carry.

exclusive-or.definition: The Boolean truth-function XOR, which returns 1 exactly when its two inputs differ.

base-case.definition: A case handled directly by a recursive definition or procedure, without another recursive call.

recursive-case.definition: A case handled by applying the same definition or procedure to smaller parts and combining their results.

set-union.definition: The union S ∪ T contains every object belonging to S or T, including objects belonging to both.

set-difference.definition: The difference S ∖ T contains the members of S that do not belong to T.

set-complement.definition: The complement W ∖ S contains the objects in a specified universe W that do not belong to S.

boolean-evaluation.definition: The extension of a Boolean valuation to all formulas of a propositional language: it keeps the assigned values of variables and interprets ¬, ∧ and ∨ using NOT, AND and OR, respectively.

boolean-value.definition: One of the two values 0 and 1. In logic, they represent false and true, respectively. The Boolean value v(A) of a formula A under a valuation v is determined by the values of its variables and the Boolean functions interpreting its connectives.

boolean-model.definition: A Boolean valuation of the propositional variables of a language, used to represent a possible reasoning situation. It is a model of a formula when that formula has value 1 under the valuation.

sat-solving.definition: Using an algorithm to decide whether a propositional formula or finite set of propositional formulas is satisfiable.

unsatisfiable.definition: A propositional formula is unsatisfiable iff no Boolean valuation makes it true. A set of formulas is unsatisfiable iff no Boolean valuation makes all of them true.

sat-problem.definition: The problem of deciding whether a given propositional formula or finite set of propositional formulas is satisfiable.

hardware-verification.definition: Checking whether a hardware implementation meets its specification.

truth-table.definition: A table listing the values of one or more propositional formulas under every assignment to their variables.

decidable.definition: A problem is decidable if an algorithm terminates on every allowed input with the correct yes-or-no answer.

time-complexity.definition: The running time of an algorithm as a function of its input size.

combinatorial-explosion.definition: Rapid growth in the number of combinations to consider as the number of choices increases.

normal-form.definition: A prescribed syntactic shape for expressions.

negation-normal-form.definition: A propositional formula built from literals using only conjunction and disjunction.

canonical-normal-form.definition: For a fixed ordered variable list, the canonical DNF lists the full terms describing true rows; the canonical CNF lists the full clauses excluding false rows. Components follow binary row order and literals follow variable order.

complementary-literals.definition: A pair consisting of a propositional variable and its negation.

resolution-pivot.definition: The variable whose positive and negative literals are removed in one resolution step.

resolvent.definition: The disjunction of the literals remaining after one complementary pair is removed from two parent clauses, with repetitions removed.

resolution-saturation.definition: A clause list is saturated under resolution iff every resolvent is tautological or already present, ignoring the order and repetition of literals.

refutation-completeness.definition: The property that every unsatisfiable input has a derivation of a contradiction in the given proof system.

tseytin-transformation.definition: A linear-size CNF encoding that gives subformulas fresh variables, constrains their values, and asserts the original formula through its name.

iff.definition: An abbreviation of “if and only if”, asserting both directions of a condition.

conjunctive-clause.definition: A conjunction of literals, also called a term. A single literal counts as a conjunctive clause.

expert-system.definition: A system for reasoning or decision making in a particular area, typically combining a knowledge base of expert rules and facts with an inference engine.

antecedent.definition: The if-part A of a conditional A → B.

consequent.definition: The then-part B of a conditional A → B.

counterfactual-conditional.definition: A conditional describing what would be the case under a supposition that may differ from the actual situation.

fact.definition: In a propositional rule base, an atom given as known information.

depth-first-search.definition: A search that follows one branch as far as possible before returning to try an alternative.

breadth-first-search.definition: A search that explores every possibility at one depth before moving to the next depth.

definite-clause.definition: A disjunctive clause containing exactly one positive literal.

goal-clause.definition: A disjunctive clause with no positive literal, expressing that its underlying atoms cannot all be true. The empty clause is included.

horn-sat.definition: The problem of deciding whether a finite conjunction of Horn clauses is satisfiable.

least-model.definition: A model whose true atoms are contained among the true atoms of every model of the same formulas.

agenda.definition: A collection of items awaiting processing by a reasoning procedure.

queue.definition: A list processed in first-in, first-out order: new items enter at the end and the first item is removed next.

plan.definition: For a fixed horizon, a model of a planning knowledge base together with its initial and goal conditions, assigning values to state and action atoms at each time point.

fluent.definition: A feature of a world whose truth may change over time; a propositional planning encoding uses a separate atom for its value at each time point.

frame-condition.definition: A formula specifying when a fluent retains its value from one time point to the next.

sat-planning.definition: Encoding an initial state, a goal, and permitted transitions over a fixed finite horizon as a propositional formula whose satisfying assignments describe plans.

frame-problem.definition: The problem of representing what remains unchanged when an action occurs without explicitly describing every unaffected feature.

prefix-notation.definition: Notation in which each operator is written before its arguments. Fixed operator arities determine how the expression is grouped.

postfix-notation.definition: Notation in which each operator is written after its arguments. Fixed operator arities determine how the expression is grouped.

infix-notation.definition: Notation in which a binary operator is written between its two arguments. Brackets or precedence conventions specify grouping.

stack.definition: A collection in which items are added and removed at one end, the top. The last item added is the first removed.

push.definition: To add an item to the top of a stack.

pop.definition: To remove and return the top item of a nonempty stack.

monotonicity.definition: The property that adding premises to a valid inference preserves its validity, with interpretations and the model space held fixed.

idempotence.definition: For a binary operation, the property that applying it to two copies of the same input returns that input.

parity.definition: Whether a whole number is even or odd. The parity of a list of bits is 0 when it contains an even number of 1s and 1 otherwise.

planning-horizon.definition: The chosen number of action steps in a bounded planning problem. A SAT encoding tests for a plan within that bound.

shunting-yard.definition: An algorithm that converts infix expressions to postfix notation, using a stack to hold operators until precedence and grouping allow them to be written to the output.

unit-clause.definition: A disjunctive clause consisting of a single literal. Satisfying it requires that literal to be true.

tautological-clause.definition: A disjunctive clause containing a literal and its negation. It is true under every valuation and imposes no constraint on a satisfying valuation.

positive-literal.definition: An unnegated atomic formula. Positive describes its syntactic form, not its truth-value.

negative-literal.definition: The negation of an atomic formula. Negative describes its syntactic form, not its truth-value.

introduction-rule.definition: An inference rule deriving a formula with the relevant connective as its main connective.

elimination-rule.definition: An inference rule using a formula with the relevant main connective to derive a conclusion.

open-assumption.definition: An assumption on which a derivation still depends.

multiple-discharge.definition: Discharging several occurrences of an assumption with the same label in one rule application.

vacuous-discharge.definition: Discharge of an assumption that was not used in the derivation.

intuitionistic-logic.definition: A logic whose natural deduction rules omit classical proof by contradiction; double-negation elimination is not generally available.

lemma.definition: A proved result used in another proof.

automated-theorem-prover.definition: Software that searches for formal proofs of specified claims from given assumptions.

kernel.definition: The component of a proof assistant that checks proofs according to its basic rules.

type.definition: A classification of terms that determines which constructions and operations are permitted on them.

typed-term.definition: An expression assigned a type by the rules of a type system; t : A states that t has type A.

constructor.definition: An operation for building a term of a type from specified inputs.

type-checking.definition: Checking whether a term has a specified type according to the rules of the type system.

proof-term.definition: A typed term representing a formal proof, whose type expresses the proposition proved.

function-symbol.definition: A symbol of fixed arity that forms an object-denoting term when applied to that many terms.

arity.definition: The number of argument places of a function or predicate symbol.

signature.definition: The constants, function symbols, and predicate symbols of a language, with a fixed arity for each function and predicate symbol.

fol-atomic-formula.definition: A predicate applied to the appropriate number of terms, or an identity between two terms.

quantifier-scope.definition: The formula that is the immediate child of a quantifier in a syntax tree.

open-formula.definition: A formula with at least one free variable occurrence.

fol-model.definition: A nonempty domain with a denotation for each constant, a total function for each function symbol, and a relation for each predicate symbol.

knowledge-graph.definition: A graph representing objects as nodes and relations among them through labeled links.

variable-assignment.definition: A mapping from variables to objects in the domain of a model.

satisfaction.definition: The relation between a model, a variable assignment, and a formula that is true under that assignment in the model.

truth-in-a-model.definition: A sentence is true in a model if it is satisfied under every variable assignment in that model.

relational-database.definition: A database that stores relations as tables.

relational-query.definition: A request for the assignments to a formula’s free variables that satisfy it in a database model.

relational-calculus.definition: A language for relational queries in which variables stand for domain objects and formulas specify satisfying assignments.

relational-algebra.definition: A language that forms relational queries using operations on tables.

tuple.definition: A finite sequence of objects, with order and repetitions retained.

planning-action.definition: An operation an agent can perform in the world. An action atom states that a particular action occurs at a particular time.

assignment-prescription.definition: A list [x₁ ↦ d₁, …, xₙ ↦ dₙ] specifying values for distinct variables. When these include every free variable of a formula, they suffice to determine its satisfaction.

assignment-variant.definition: The assignment v[x ↦ d] sends x to d and agrees with v on every other variable.

model-diagram.definition: The set of all atomic and negated atomic sentences true in a model after adding a name for every domain object.

set-diagram.definition: A diagram representing sets by regions and membership by placement inside those regions.

formula-extension.definition: The set of ordered tuples of domain objects that satisfy a formula when assigned to its free variables in a specified order.

quantification.definition: The expression of how many individuals satisfy a condition. Universal and existential quantification concern all individuals and at least one individual, respectively.

finite-model.definition: A model with a finite domain.

iterated-quantifiers.definition: Quantifiers occurring within the scopes of other quantifiers.

infinite-model.definition: A model with an infinite domain.

vacuous-quantifier.definition: A quantifier whose scope contains no free occurrence of the variable it quantifies.

unifier.definition: A substitution that makes two expressions syntactically identical.

alpha-renaming.definition: Changing a bound variable and its bound occurrences to a fresh variable without changing meaning.

currying.definition: Representing a function of several arguments as nested functions, each taking one argument.

dependent-function.definition: A function whose output type can depend on its input.

existential-witness.definition: An object that satisfies the quantified scope of an existential claim.

fol-clause.definition: A finite disjunction of first-order literals, with all free variables universally quantified; the empty disjunction is ⊥.

fol-cnf.definition: A conjunction of first-order clauses, each with its free variables understood as universally quantified.

fol-consequence.definition: A formula C is a first-order consequence of premises Γ if every first-order model and variable assignment satisfying all formulas in Γ also satisfies C.

fol-literal.definition: An atomic first-order formula or its negation.

fol-resolution.definition: An inference from freshly renamed clauses with opposite-sign literals whose atoms unify, deleting those literals and applying their most general unifier to the remaining literals.

free-for.definition: A term is free for a variable in a formula when substituting it for that variable captures none of the term’s variables.

halting-problem.definition: The problem of determining whether a given program will eventually stop on a given input.

skolem-constant.definition: A fresh constant used as an existential witness with no universally quantified variables in scope.

skolem-function.definition: A fresh function symbol used to choose an existential witness as a function of the universally quantified variables in scope.

standardizing-apart.definition: Renaming variables in separate clause uses so that those uses have disjoint variable sets.

undecidable.definition: A decision problem is undecidable when no algorithm terminates on every input and correctly answers every instance.

universal-closure.definition: The sentence obtained by universally quantifying all free variables of a formula.

fol-sat.definition: The problem of determining whether a given finite set of first-order sentences has a model.

fol-satisfiability.definition: A set of first-order sentences is satisfiable if some first-order model makes all of them true.
